# Does a Shorter Working Week Raise Productivity? A Synthesis of Five Sources

*Evidence briefing. Prepared for a working group on working-time policy.*

## Purpose

This briefing weighs five pieces of evidence on whether reducing the working week by a fifth, with pay maintained, raises productivity: the Halden multi-organisation pilot (source 1), the Varden County randomised trial at nine months (source 2), a re-analysis of the Halden pilot (source 3), a meta-analysis of 23 studies (source 4), and the 24-month follow-up of the Varden trial and of 14 Halden organisations (source 5). It adds no new data. Its aim is to state what the five together support, at the strength they support it, and what they leave open.

## 1. What each source contributes, and how later sources qualify it

**Source 1** established that many organisations that volunteered could cut scheduled hours by 20% with little change in reported output, and reported a 23.4% gain in output per hour, gains in every sector, large falls in sickness and resignations, and 92% continuation. Taken alone, it suggests a large, general effect.

**Source 2** was the first randomised evidence, with record-based output and actual hours. It introduced the distinction that the rest of the body depends on: between discretionary work, where output can be produced at any time within a deadline, and coverage-bound work, where output depends on presence while demand arrives. Per actual hour, output rose 12.5% in case-processing and 6.7% in counter work; per employee it was roughly unchanged in the first and fell 11.4% in the second. It also showed that actual hours fall less than scheduled hours, and that dividing by scheduled hours inflated the case-processing estimate from 12.5% to 22%.

**Source 3** found that source 1's figures were inflated in several documented ways: seven of nine withdrawals occurred after the schedule began, mostly for workload reasons, not "during the preparation phase"; manager-reported output exceeded record-based output by 3.8 points; actual hours fell 14.1%, not 20%; and the 1.4% revenue rise was a real fall of about 2.6% after inflation of 4.1%. Correcting what could be corrected reduced the per-hour gain to 10.8% in a subset. These findings stand. Source 3 then went further, concluding that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact, attributing the remainder to novelty on the basis of an extrapolated survey trend, and dismissing source 2's meetings hypothesis as post hoc. Those further claims do not survive later evidence.

**Source 4** placed both studies in a wider literature. Its pooled per-hour estimate of 13.4% is inflated by the same features source 3 identified; the estimates from controlled designs (+8.2%), actual-hours studies (+7.9%), record-based studies (+9.7%), controlled discretionary studies (+9.6%) and bias adjustment (+9.1%) converge on roughly 8 to 10%. Its work-type moderator generalises source 2: per-worker output fell about 9% in coverage-bound settings, consistently, and was roughly maintained in discretionary ones. It rejected source 1's sector-general claim and source 3's artifact claim. Its own claim that effects show no decay was wrong, for the reason source 5 gives.

**Source 5** applied the strictest standards in the body: randomisation, record-based output, log-measured hours and a two-year horizon. The per-hour gain in case-processing declined from 12.5% to 8.5% (log hours) but remained clearly above zero. Output per employee stood at −3.4%, with a confidence interval including zero. A registered mediation test attributed 47% of the gain to fewer recurring meetings and 18% to reduced fatigue. Source 4's "no decay" conclusion rested on four long-follow-up studies, all uncontrolled and using scheduled hours. The counter arm was ended at month 12.

## 2. Weighing the estimates

**Table 1. Estimates of the change in output per hour, ordered by strength of design**

| Estimate | Source | Change per hour |
|---|---|---|
| Uncontrolled, manager-reported, scheduled hours | 1 | +23.4% |
| Uncontrolled survivors, records, actual hours, 24 months | 5 | +11.8% |
| Uncontrolled subset, records, actual hours, 6 months | 3 | +10.8% |
| Meta-analysis, all studies | 4 | +13.4% |
| Meta-analysis, bias-adjusted | 4 | +9.1% |
| Meta-analysis, controlled discretionary | 4 | +9.6% |
| Randomised, case-processing, 9 months, timesheets | 2 | +12.5% |
| Randomised, case-processing, 24 months, system logs | 5 | +8.5% |
| Randomised, counter work, 9 months | 2 | +6.7% |

Estimates fall as designs strengthen and stabilise around 8 to 10% for discretionary work. The figure of more than 20% is not supported by any design that measures actual hours.

## 3. What the body supports

Read as a whole, the five sources support a conditional answer.

1. **Per hour, yes, by a moderate amount.** In discretionary work, a 20% cut in scheduled hours raises output per actual hour by roughly 8 to 10% under controlled measurement, with some decline from the first year to the second but no sign of disappearing within two years. The headline figure of more than 20% is an artifact of scheduled-hours denominators, manager-reported output and selection.
2. **Per worker, no.** Because actual hours fall by 11 to 14%, not 20%, a per-hour gain of 8 to 10% roughly offsets the hours cut but does not exceed it. Output per worker in discretionary work is around 2 to 4% lower than it would have been, with intervals that include zero. "Same output in four days" is close to true there; "more output" is not supported.
3. **In coverage-bound work, the answer is no on any measure that matters to the people served.** Output per worker falls by about 9 to 11%, waits lengthen, and maintaining service requires about 12% more staff. Per-hour gains exist but are small. This is the most consistent finding in the body.
4. **About half the per-hour gain in the best-measured setting comes from removing recurring meetings**, a smaller part from reduced fatigue, and about a third is unexplained.
5. **Sickness absence and resignations fall substantially** in every source that measured them (by roughly 27 to 36% for sick days). These are real benefits, but they are not themselves productivity, and the body does not estimate how far they offset per-worker output losses.

Whether "productivity" rises therefore depends on whether it is measured per hour or per worker, and on whether output in a given role depends on presence. Both slogans, "a four-day week makes people more productive" and "the gains are a mirage", are wrong as stated.

## 4. What the body leaves open

- **Is the hours cut necessary for the gain?** About half the per-hour gain runs through cutting meetings. Two control offices that audited meetings without cutting hours saw a 4.1% per-hour rise, but that is two offices without a comparison group. No study had an arm that reorganised work without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone would capture much of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and last, is not settled by this body.
- **Beyond two years.** No controlled evidence extends past 24 months. The per-hour gain declined between 9 and 24 months; whether it stabilises or continues to decline is unknown.
- **The unexplained third** of the per-hour gain has no tested mechanism.
- **Manufacturing and shift production** are almost absent from the evidence (two studies, both mixed).
- **Private-sector controlled evidence** is thin; the strongest designs are in public administration.

## 5. Bottom line

A 20% cut in scheduled hours at full pay raises output per hour by roughly 8 to 10% in discretionary work, about half of it through fewer meetings, which roughly but not fully offsets the hours lost; in coverage-bound work it reduces output and service unless staff are added. Whether the gain requires the hours cut, or could be had by reorganising work alone, remains open.

response:
# Review of "Does a Shorter Working Week Raise Productivity? A Synthesis of Five Sources"

**Bottom line:** This is a good briefing. Its overall structure is right: a moderate per-hour gain in discretionary work, losses in coverage-bound work, and the main open question being whether the hours cut is necessary at all. It also handles the two overreaching papers (sources 3 and 4) fairly.

Its main weakness is that it repeats some of the overstatements its sources made, and in places sharpens them:
- it mixes hours measures when describing the decline;
- it states the meetings mechanism as established;
- it treats overlapping estimates as independent confirmation;
- it leaves out cost, which a policy working group will need most.

## Where the briefing misstates its sources

**1. "Declined from 12.5% to 8.5% (log hours)" (§1, source 5).** This repeats the error in source 5's own summary. The 12.5% figure uses timesheets; the 8.5% uses system logs. The like-for-like comparison is 12.5% → 9.8% on timesheets, with 8.5% on the stricter log measure at 24 months. The cross-measure comparison makes the decline look larger than it was.

**2. "Its own claim that effects show no decay was wrong" (source 4).** Source 5 showed the meta-analysis's long-follow-up studies couldn't support that claim, because all four were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. That makes the claim *unsupported*, not wrong. The Varden decline itself was never formally tested, and its 9-month and 24-month intervals overlap heavily. "Was unsupported" is the accurate wording.

**3. "Source 2 was the first randomised evidence."** Source 4 includes three randomised studies spanning 1998–2025, with Varden as one of them. Nothing in the five sources shows Varden came first. Similarly, "introduced the distinction" overstates it, since source 1 already discussed customer-facing sectors. "The first randomised evidence in this body, and the source that made the distinction central" would be accurate.

**4. Source 3's novelty claim is treated as simply refuted.** Its claim that the gain would reach zero by month ten was refuted. But source 5 found some decline, which is the direction source 3 predicted. A fairer summary: source 3 was right that some of the early gain fades, and wrong that all of it does.

**5. "Same output in four days" is close to true (§3.2).** Staff didn't work four days. Actual hours fell 11–14%, not 20%, partly through work on the day off and longer remaining days. The accurate phrasing is "nearly the same output with about 12% fewer actual hours." The difference matters for anyone promising staff a genuine four-day week.

## Where the briefing claims more than the evidence supports

**6. The convergence on "8 to 10%" isn't five independent confirmations.** Several of those estimates share underlying studies:
- **Within the meta-analysis:** the controlled, actual-hours, record-based and controlled-discretionary subgroups overlap heavily. Six of the eight actual-hours studies are controlled, for example.
- **Across sources:** Varden is itself one of the meta-analysis's studies, so the randomised and meta-analytic estimates aren't independent either.
- **What the figure rests on:** the strongest evidence for 8–10% in discretionary work is one public employer, with seven treated and seven control offices.

That figure is the best available estimate, but the briefing should say how narrow its base is.

**7. "About half the per-hour gain comes from removing recurring meetings" (§3.4 and the bottom line).** This is stated as established, and the bottom line extends it to discretionary work in general. Its actual basis is narrower:
- it was a single registered analysis, in the same seven offices that first suggested the idea;
- meeting cuts weren't randomised, so the mediation result depends on assumptions that can't be checked;
- the effective sample is 14 offices.

There is also a measurement question. In my review of source 5, I noted that the system-log measure and the meeting data don't fit together as described. On rough accounting, meetings could explain more than half of the gain, not less. "In the one setting tested, fewer meetings appear to be the largest single pathway" would be accurate.

**8. Per-hour gains in coverage-bound work (§3.3).** The briefing treats these as real but small. When opening hours stay fixed and fewer staff are present, queues absorb the idle time between customers. Output per staffed hour then rises with no one working faster, and the public's waiting time pays for it. The briefing should note that the per-hour figure there probably reflects busier staff, not productivity.

**9. The 12% extra staffing figure.** This is one county's estimate for its own counter offices. The briefing presents it as a general requirement for coverage-bound work.

**10. Table 1 isn't monotonic.** "Estimates fall as designs strengthen" is only roughly true:
- the randomised 9-month estimate (12.5%) exceeds the meta-analysis's controlled-discretionary estimate (9.6%);
- it also exceeds two uncontrolled subset estimates (10.8% and 11.8%);
- the table mixes discretionary and coverage-bound work, nine-month and two-year results, and different hours measures.

Splitting the table by work type, or adding columns for hours measure and follow-up length, would make the pattern clearer and more honest.

## What the briefing leaves out

**11. Cost.** For a working group this is the most important omission. Pay is unchanged and output per worker falls about 3% in discretionary work. So labour cost per unit of output rises by roughly 3–4%, before any overtime. In coverage-bound work, one county estimated about 9% higher cost per contact to restore service. The briefing should state these figures directly, alongside the possibility that lower sickness and turnover offsets part of the cost. The latter has not been estimated.

**12. Backlogs and service in discretionary work.** No source reports backlog, time to decision, or deadline compliance. Steady output per worker in queue-based work could hide a slowly growing backlog. That belongs in §4.

**13. The discretionary/coverage split isn't clean.** In the Halden follow-up, a marketing agency reverted over client deadlines, and that is discretionary work. The briefing's own Limitations note that organisations mix both kinds of work. Policy guidance should treat work type as a feature of individual roles, not of whole sectors or organisations.

**14. Varden's 24-month estimate is probably slightly understated.** Two control offices cut their meetings from month 15. That narrows the gap between treated and control offices, so the 8.5% figure is if anything conservative. This is worth one sentence.

**15. Resignations.** Lower resignations have an obvious alternative explanation: staff don't leave an employer offering a shorter week at full pay. They may reflect the value of the benefit rather than improved wellbeing. The sick-leave reduction is better supported, since Varden measured it against a randomised control group.

## Suggested revised bottom line

> In the best evidence available, from one public employer and supported by a wider but weaker literature, a 20% cut in scheduled hours at full pay reduced actual hours by about 12% and raised output per actual hour by roughly 8 to 10% in work that can be done at any time within a deadline. Output per worker was about 3% lower, so labour cost per unit of output rose slightly, partly offset by lower sickness absence. Part of the gain appears to come from cutting recurring meetings. In work that depends on staff being present when the public arrives, output and service fell, and restoring them required more staff at higher cost. Whether the gains need the hours cut at all, or could be had by reorganising work alone, has not been tested, and no controlled evidence extends beyond two years.

The open question in §4, whether reorganisation alone could capture the gain, is the right note to end on. A three-arm trial would answer it: reduced hours, reorganisation without reduced hours, and control. That would be the single most useful recommendation the working group could make.

I can produce a revised version of the full briefing with these changes, or a one-page version for non-specialist members of the working group.
